title: Graph learning found a fairness–cooperation link in a British survey sample
summary: A learned graph fitted to 1,805 Great Britain responses in the European Social Survey consistently linked perceived police procedural fairness with willingness to cooperate. The link appeared in all 20 near-best graph classes, whereas the link between moral alignment and cooperation was uncertain. Directions in the reported ordered graph came from the researchers' theory-based ordering, so the findings describe relationships in survey responses.
ai_technology: DAGGLE; latent Gaussian graph structure learning
organization: East China Normal University; London School of Economics and Political Science

source_review.scope: Original arXiv v1 abstract and history, HTML §3 and European Social Survey §§6.1–6.3; earlier related DAG-CLIP primary abstract

evidence.tested: The study examined 15 survey measures and five latent constructs. It compared candidates with the published structural equation model and exhaustively assessed the small graph-class space in addition to the fitted search. The fairness–cooperation association was retained with the same sign in reported subgroup fits under the specified ordering.
evidence.unknown: The associations are retrospective and model-dependent. The data do not identify the direction of the fairness–cooperation relationship, or show that changing policing would cause a change in willingness to cooperate.
evidence.ai_role: DAGGLE learned latent-construct adjacency structure jointly with measurement and structural parameters. It used likelihood-based edge screening and comparison across graph equivalence classes; theory supplied any reported link orientation.
